title: Russia outlines new digital depository rules ahead of fall crypto framework roll-out
dek: Russia's central bank has published draft regulations establishing tiered capital requirements from $570,000 to $2.8 million for digital asset platforms ahead of a full crypto framework launching in September. The move signals institutional integration of digital assets into the financial system but arrives amid EU sanctions targeting Russian crypto firms.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: Settlement depositories will require 250 million rubles ($2.8 million) in liquid capital, with tiered requirements down to $570,000 for other digital depositories, according to the Bank of Russia's draft regulations.
bottom_line: Russia's central bank publishes draft regulations establishing capital requirements ($2.8M liquid capital) and organized trading rules for digital assets ahead of broader crypto framework launch.
body: The Bank of Russia has published draft regulations that would establish tiered capital requirements for digital asset platforms ahead of a broader cryptocurrency framework scheduled to launch in September. The proposals represent the central bank's first formal effort to create organized cryptocurrency markets by extending existing securities market rules to digital assets, but the framework is being rolled out amid concurrent European Union sanctions targeting Russian-linked crypto firms.

The regulations would create "digital depositories," regulated companies responsible for recording holdings of cryptocurrencies and other digital assets. Settlement depositories, the highest tier, would require 250 million rubles, roughly $2.8 million, in liquid capital, according to CoinDesk's reporting on the Bank of Russia announcement. Firms that control crypto addresses or hold assets with foreign custodians would face a mid-tier requirement of 100 million rubles, approximately $1.1 million. Other digital depositories would require 50 million rubles, about $570,000.

Assets counted toward these capital requirements must be liquid, while eligible financial assets must meet the central bank's credit-quality standards. The same capital requirements would apply to operators of electronic platforms that settle transactions involving digital financial assets. The central bank will maintain registers of digital depositories, crypto exchange operators, and companies that issue digital financial assets under the framework.

The regulatory structure mirrors Russia's existing securities market architecture, suggesting an intent to integrate digital assets into the formal financial system rather than isolate them. The draft regulations were created under a digital assets bill adopted by the State Duma on July 21 and approved by the Federation Council on July 24. The proposals have not yet been finalized and have been released for public assessment.

The timing creates a striking contradiction. Four days before the Bank of Russia's digital asset rule announcements, the European Union unveiled its 21st sanction package targeting 14 crypto firms, according to CoinDesk. That package included A7, described as a $120 billion stablecoin network. The sanctions suggest geopolitical friction around Russia's integration of cryptocurrency into its financial infrastructure even as domestic regulation proceeds.

The capital thresholds may reshape the Russian crypto market structure by excluding smaller platforms that cannot meet the $570,000 minimum threshold. This could centralize activity among larger players with sufficient capital reserves. The liquidity requirements, tied to the central bank's credit-quality standards, introduce regulatory discretion that could be used to restrict certain asset classes or foreign custodians. The proposals remain in draft form, and final implementation details are still uncertain heading into the September rollout target.

The Bottom Line: Russia is formalizing crypto regulation through capital and organizational requirements that parallel its securities framework, but the EU's simultaneous sanctions on Russian crypto firms signal that geopolitical and regulatory pressures are colliding. Watch for which platforms meet the capital thresholds and how the central bank defines "liquid" assets and credit-quality standards in the final rules.
